segments.01-problem: Telegram bots get tested by hand. You open Telegram, send slash start, tap a button, scroll, type a phone number... and you do it all again after every change. Unit tests mock the Bot API, so they never see what a user sees: a button that does nothing, a keyboard that never goes away, a reply that only breaks in a real group.
segments.02-what: BotProof changes that. You describe each user journey in plain English, in a Kane test file. Kane CLI, from TestMu AI, then drives the real Telegram Web client in Chrome, logged in as a dedicated test account, and checks what a person would actually see. No mocks. No shortcuts through the Bot API.
segments.03-private: Here is Kane working through Brew Bot, our demo coffee bot. It sends slash start and checks the formatted welcome and its buttons. It opens the menu, taps Next, and verifies that the same message was edited in place, not sent again. Then it opens a drink, checks the link button, and reads the alert that pops up when you add it.
segments.03b-miniapp: It even tests the Mini App. Kane confirms an order, taps Checkout, and the Mini App opens inside Telegram. It picks a pickup time, presses Telegram's own Pay button, and checks that the bot received the order and confirmed the payment in the chat.
segments.04-group-channel: The same bot, in a group and in a channel. Kane starts a group order and taps a drink, and the bot edits its message to show who ordered what. In the channel, the bot posts today's special, edits it, and deletes it, and Kane checks every change.
segments.05-bug-loop: Now the part unit tests miss. In our test group, the account posts as an anonymous admin. When it sent slash close, the bot replied: only group admins can close the order. To the group's own owner. Telegram delivers an anonymous admin's message from a placeholder account, and the bot was asking whether that placeholder was an admin. It never is. BotProof's fix loop handed Claude Code the failing step, Kane's remark, the screenshot, and the bot's source. Claude may only edit bot code: the test files and BotProof itself are locked, by a hook and by a git check. It changed one condition. BotProof redeployed the bot to Vercel, Kane ran the flow again, and it passed. Every attempt, and its diff, is in the run log.
segments.06-close: The loop also knows when not to patch. When Telegram itself got in the way, a tip covering the screen, or a client still reconnecting, Kane's triage blamed the automation, not the bot, and the bot was left untouched. Every run ends in a sealed Kane evidence pack, so anyone can replay exactly what happened, without logging in. Your bot works on your laptop. BotProof proves it works in Telegram.
